Great — rearranging is a good weekend project. Below are practical, concrete tips you can use, with a few items tailored to things you’ve mentioned (Echo Show / smart bulbs, weak bedroom Wi‑Fi, a walnut mid‑century dresser, and trying to reduce screens before bed).

Before you start
- Measure the room, door swing(s), windows, radiator/vents, and current furniture (width/depth/height). Sketch a few scale layouts on paper or use a free room planner app.  
- Clear enough floor space to test layouts easily. Wear work gloves and have at least one helper for heavy pieces.

Bed placement (priority)
- Make the bed the focal point: center it on the longest wall that isn’t directly under a window or blocking the door. That usually feels most restful and balanced.
- Leave at least 24–30 in (60–75 cm) of clear walkway on each side if possible for comfortable access.
- Avoid placing the bed directly under an air vent or where cold drafts hit.

Storage & dresser placement
- Put your walnut mid‑century dresser on a wall where it’s visible but doesn’t block natural light or walkways. A dresser under a wall mirror or a simple framed piece above it looks classic.
- Leave some clearance to open drawers fully; measure drawer swing before committing to a spot.
- Keep frequently used items closer to the closet/door; seasonal or less-used items can go on top/back of dresser.

Create a sleep‑friendly zone
- Keep electronics off or out of reach of the bed to help with your goal of reducing evening screen time (you mentioned DND after 10 PM). A small basket or charger station on the dresser works well.
- If you enjoy reading, make a cozy reading nook with a small chair, side table, and a warm, dimmable task lamp (your Echo Show can still control smart bulbs nearby).

Lighting & smart home
- Use layered lighting: overhead, bedside lamps, and a dimmable reading lamp. Warm color temps in the evening help sleep.  
- Keep your Echo Show in a spot where voice control for smart bulbs is convenient, but not too near the bed if it tempts you to stay up.

Wi‑Fi & electronics (specific to your weak bedroom signal)
- Don’t rely on the living‑room range extender alone if the bedroom still has weak signal. Options:
  - Add a mesh Wi‑Fi node in/near the bedroom (best performance, seamless roaming).
  - Or place a wired (Ethernet) access point or Powerline adapter + Wi‑Fi node in the bedroom.
  - If you move the router higher (you were planning that), it can help; but putting a mesh node where you sleep is the most reliable fix.
- Keep Wi‑Fi gear off the floor and away from big metal objects. Avoid putting extenders/routers inside closed cabinets.
- If you’ll rearrange electronics, plan outlet locations and where the Echo Show will sit for both voice control and best Wi‑Fi reception.

Cable management & tech organization
- Use cable sleeves, adhesive cable clips, and a small cable box or under‑desk tray to hide power strips. Velcro ties make rearranging easy.
- Label cords so you can reconnect quickly after moving furniture.
- If you have a TV or computer area in the bedroom, use a surge protector with enough outlets and a long enough cord for the new layout.

Aesthetics & mid‑century touches
- Keep surfaces relatively uncluttered to highlight the walnut dresser and brass accents you like. A simple mirror or minimalist artwork above the dresser enhances the mid‑century look.
- Use a neutral rug with a geometric pattern or subtle texture; scale it so the front legs of furniture sit on it.
- Keep hardware simple and proportional (you already prefer simple brass knobs — good choice).

Practical moving tips & safety
- Use furniture sliders to move heavy pieces without scratching floors. Lift with legs, not back. Get help for tall/heavy items and anchor tall dressers to the wall.
- Protect floors with drop cloths if you’re testing many layouts.

Weekend checklist (rough timing)
- 30 min: measure and sketch 2–3 layouts.
- 60–90 min: clear room and test furniture positions.
- 60 min: move and set major pieces (with help).
- 30–60 min: set up lighting and electronics; test Wi‑Fi in key spots.
- 30 min: cable management and styling (mirrors, small decor).

Likely reasons
- Drafting/paceline effect: riding in a group cuts aerodynamic drag a lot. If you’re tucked in the pack you can save ~20–40% of the power needed to hold the same speed, so the bike (and speed) will feel much easier.
- Different pacing/steady speed: group rides tend to have fewer stop–gos and more sustained speeds, which is more efficient than repeated accelerations.
- Increased motivation: adrenaline, competitive pacing, and sticking to the group make you push harder without noticing, improving performance.
- Cadence/technique: following others often smooths out cadence and gear choice, improving drivetrain efficiency.
- Environmental conditions: tailwind, milder temps, or smoother roads commonly used for group routes can boost speed/feel.
- Mechanical/thermal effects: a new chain/cassette and a warmed-up drivetrain reduce friction — running at group speed warms components and lubricant, lowering resistance.
- Bike setup differences: you may ride with slightly higher tire pressure, cleaner drivetrain, or different gear choices on group days.

How to check and confirm
- Compare ride data on your Garmin/Strava: look at average speed, heart rate, cadence, and (if available) power or estimated power. If speed is higher while heart rate or power is lower, that’s drafting/efficiency.
- Compare the same route solo vs group on similar weather days (same tire pressure, no tailwind) to isolate the effect.
- Note wind direction/temperature on both rides — tailwinds or warmer temps matter.
- Observe perceived exertion: if you’re doing more work but feel fine, it’s likely motivation/pacing.
- If you have or can borrow a power meter, that’s the cleanest way to quantify how much less power you’re producing in the group.

Quick maintenance checks (if you suspect a mechanical reason)
- Clean and lube the chain, check chain wear and cassette for damage.
- Check tire pressure and ensure brakes aren’t rubbing.
- Spin wheels for bearing/resistance or freehub issues.

What you can do with this
- Use group rides for higher-quality training (intervals, tempo) if you want performance gains.
- Replicate group conditions on solo days by using paceline drills, group training apps, or structured intervals to get similar physiological benefits.
- Use your Garmin data to track and learn which factors (wind, cadence, drafting) give the biggest improvements.

- Avoid letting battery sit at 0% routinely; avoid constant 100%→0% full cycles.

Quick principles
- Change one variable at a time (subject, scale, palette, tool, time limit) so experimentation feels manageable.  
- Use constraints to force creative solutions (e.g., only 3 colors, or only palette knife).  
- Build small, doable rituals (10–30 minute warmups) so momentum accumulates.

Specific inspiration prompts and exercises
1. Flower Remix: pick two flower photos you love and combine them into one imagined bloom. Push realism by inventing a stem/lighting that ties them together.  
2. Palette-knife texture study: make three 8x10 studies using only palette-knife marks — one focused on opaque layering, one on scraping/backlighting, one on heavy impasto.  
3. Limited-palette challenge: paint the same subject 3 times using 3 different 3-color palettes + white. Notice how color decisions change mood.  
4. Invert-and-paint: take a photo, invert its values in your phone, and paint what you see (great for rethinking value relationships).  
5. 30–60 minute “no-plan” warmup: set a timer, make fast marks, resist editing. Keep or crop the best bits for later.  
6. Texture swap: paint a small study on an unusual surface — cardboard, wood panel, textured fabric — and/or add mediums (modeling paste, coarse gesso) for new textures.  
7. Music-as-mood: play a playlist (e.g., David Gilmour-style guitar for spacious color; upbeat for saturated color) and paint to the song’s arc. Let tempo inform brushwork.  
8. Cross-pollination: translate a photograph of fabric, rust, or skin texture into a floral study — treat petals like folds, or vice versa.  
9. Scale flip: if you usually work small, make a very large gestural piece; if usually large, try tiny postcards. Scale changes decisions instantly.  
10. Rework an old painting: pick an unfinished or unsold piece and repaint sections, add collage, or scrape it back to find new composition.  
11. Daily photo scavenger hunt: take 5 photos a day of textures, colors, or compositions. After a week, pick one to develop into a painting.  
12. Artist mash-up: pick two artists you admire and try a one-hour piece combining their approaches (e.g., Turner lighting + a contemporary palette-knife floral).  
13. Collaboration/critique: swap works-in-progress with another painter for a week or join a local/online critique group for fresh eyes.  
14. Constraint game: paint using only 2 brushes or only palette knife + rigger. Constraints generate unusual marks.

Studio and process tweaks
- Change your light source or orientation of the painting while you work.  
- Rearrange your space: even moving the easel to a different wall can change perspective.  
- Photograph different crops of a painting and use the cropped view as a new composition starter. (If you want, I can give tips to improve phone photos of paintings.)

- Public accountability: post one progress pic a week or commit to a weekly challenge (you already like the 30-day idea — try a themed 7-day mini-challenge).

Nice — fun trip ahead. Here’s a practical checklist you can use in the store, plus a few tips tied to things you’ve mentioned (Les Paul vs Strat, open D, coil-splitting, fingerpicking).

Quick prep
- Bring a tuner and a strap (or ask to use the store’s).  
- Bring a couple of your favorite picks and your phone to record sound or take photos/serial numbers.  
- Know your budget and whether you want new or used.

What to play and how to test
- Play the same simple riffs and chords on every guitar so you can compare feel and tone. Include something you fingerpick (e.g., the Blackbird-style pattern) and a chunky rhythm so you hear split-pickup behavior.  
- Try each guitar both plugged in and unplugged. Unplugged resonance gives a lot of info for fingerpicking/acoustic-like tone.  
- If you plan to use open D often, ask to tune one guitar to open D (store may oblige) so you can test string tension, chord voicings and resonance in that tuning.

Feel & playability
- Check neck shape and thickness (comfort while fretting, thumb position).  
- Check action (string height) and fret access/feel — play high up the neck to check for buzzing or dead spots.  
- Test playability sitting and standing (weight distribution matters—Les Pauls are heavier).  
- Try different string gauges if possible; lighter gauges help fingerpicking but change tone.

Setup, frets & intonation
- Check intonation across the neck: play open string, then 12th-fret harmonic and fretted 12th note.  
- Look for fret buzz or dead frets, and check that frets are level.  
- Check truss rod access and range (ask if it’s been recently set up).  
- Ask when it was last set up (or plan to budget for a professional setup).

Pickups & electronics
- Compare pickup voicings: humbuckers (Les Paul) vs single-coils (Strat) — warm and thick vs bright and snappy.  
- If you want versatility, try guitars with coil-splitting/coiltap to get single-coil-ish tones from humbuckers. Test the split in both neck and bridge positions.  
- Turn knobs and flip switches while amplified to check for crackling/pots noise and switch reliability.  
- Listen for microphonics or unwanted noise at different volumes and pickup settings.

Hardware & construction
- Check tuners for smoothness and stability.  
- Check bridge and saddle condition; tremolo systems should feel stable if present.  
- Inspect finish for cracks, dents, or patches (especially on used guitars).  
- On Les Pauls, check weight and balance (neck dive, how it sits on a strap).

Sound through an amp
- Play through an amp you’ll use or something representative of your style. Try clean and a couple of overdrive settings—listen for clarity and note separation.  
- If you use effects, test with them as well (reverb, delay, compression, etc.). Record a short clip if allowed so you can listen later.

Practical stuff & policy
- Ask about warranty, return policy, and setup included (some stores do a basic setup).  
- For used instruments, ask about history/repairs and check serial numbers.  
- Check case or gig bag condition and whether it’s included.

Final tips
- Trust your hands: comfort and inspiration > specs.  
- Compare several guitars in the same price range — small differences can become big in feel/tone.  
- If torn between two, sleep on it and listen to your recordings the next day.

Short answer
- If you need a central, always-on backup and easier access to files now → buy now.
- If you can keep using your external drive and it’s not urgent → you can wait for a sale or a new model, and save some money.

Why buy now
- Immediate convenience and safety: a NAS will let you back up your laptop and phone automatically and serve files to devices without constant manual transfers.
- Better workflow: easier media streaming, remote access (when configured securely), and centralized backups for multiple devices.
- Beginner-friendly models are mature and easy to set up (Synology and QNAP have good UIs and guides).
- Drives and NAS hardware aren’t changing so fast that buying now will be a bad decision for typical home use.

Why you might wait
- Sales: big discounts often hit Prime Day (summer), back-to-school (late summer), and Black Friday (Nov). Waiting for one of these can save 10–30% on hardware or bundle deals.
- If you don’t urgently need more storage or automation, continuing with your external backup is safe for a while.
- If you expect to need much larger capacity or advanced features (virtual machines, heavy Plex transcoding), you might wait and research 4‑bay models or higher‑end units.

Practical guidance (for a beginner)
- 2‑bay vs 4‑bay:
  - 2‑bay: simpler, cheaper, enough for most home users who want automatic backups, media streaming, and redundancy with RAID1.
  - 4‑bay: choose if you want more raw capacity, plan to use RAID5/6, run VMs, host many services, or want easier future expansion.
- Drive choice: use NAS-rated drives (WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf). Buy two identical drives for RAID1 in a 2‑bay.
- Important: RAID is redundancy, not a backup. Keep at least one offline or offsite backup (external drive or cloud).
- Security tips: enable automatic updates, use strong passwords, enable 2‑factor auth, use encrypted shared folders if sensitive, restrict remote access (use VPN), and consider a small UPS for the NAS.

Model suggestions (beginner-friendly)
- 2‑bay: Synology DiskStation DS220+ (very user friendly), or QNAP TS‑230 (budget). Both fine for backups and light media streaming.
- 4‑bay (if you want expandability): Synology DS420+ or QNAP TS‑453D.

Estimated cost (diskless 2‑bay)
- NAS box: ~$200–$400
- Drives: ~$60–$100 per TB (prices vary) — two 4TB NAS drives is a common starter choice
- Total starting budget: roughly $350–$700

What to do if you decide to wait
- Continue regular backups to your external drive and consider a secondary offsite/cloud copy for critical data.
- Monitor upcoming sale dates (Prime Day/back-to-school/Black Friday) and product news for new NAS releases.

Great — here are focused, practical tips and quick fixes that will help your slow-cooker meals come out better and more reliably.

Top general rules
- Fill level: aim for about 1/2 to 2/3 full. Too empty = temperature swings; too full = undercooked center.
- Keep the lid on. Every time you lift it you drop the temp and add 15–30 minutes (or more) of cook time.
- Low vs High: low for long, gentle braises (8–10 hrs); high for quicker meals (4–6 hrs). If you have time, choose low for more tender results.
- Safety: check internal temps with a thermometer. Poultry 165°F (74°C). For shreddable pork/beef, cook until 190–205°F (88–96°C).

Prep and flavor
- Sear first. Brown meat and sauté aromatics in a skillet, then deglaze with a little liquid and add to the slow cooker. That adds lots of flavor.
- Deglaze the pan and add the liquid — don’t pour browned bits down the drain.
- Use bone-in cuts and fattier pieces for better flavor and less dryness.
- Layer smartly: dense root veg (carrots, potatoes) on the bottom, then meat, then softer veg on top.

Vegetables and timing
- Cut veg larger for long cooks so they don’t turn to mush. Add quick-cooking veggies (bell pepper, peas, zucchini) in the last 30–60 minutes.
- For soups/stews you prefer chunkier veg, cut them large and/or add some at the end.

Liquid and consistency
- You usually need less liquid than stovetop recipes; slow cookers don’t lose much steam. Start with enough to barely cover solids if you want a stew-like result.
- If result is too thin: remove lid and cook on high to reduce, blend some cooked veg into the sauce, or thicken with a cornstarch slurry (mix cold water + cornstarch; add and cook 10–20 minutes) or instant mashed potato flakes.
- If too watery: skim fat and reduce, or thicken as above.

Seasoning and finishing
- Season lightly at the start, then adjust salt and acid at the end. Long cooking can mute salt and acidity.
- Add delicate herbs and fresh greens near the end. Dried herbs do well added early.
- Toast whole spices in a pan before adding for more depth.

Beans and legumes
- Canned beans are the easiest and most reliable. If using dried beans, pre-soak and boil kidney beans for 10 minutes before slow-cooking to destroy toxins (important).
- If using dried beans without pre-soak, they may take a long time and cook unevenly.

Dairy and eggs
- Add milk, cream, yogurt and cheese near the end of cooking to avoid curdling or separation.
- For slow-cooker yogurt: heat milk to ~180°F (82°C), cool to ~110°F (43°C) before adding starter — using a thermometer helps a lot.

Troubleshooting common problems
- Meat dry/tough: likely cooked too long on high or was a lean cut. Use lower temp, add a fatty cut or a little more liquid, or switch to a different cut next time.
- Meat undercooked: pieces were too large or not enough time/temperature. Cut into smaller chunks and check temp.
- Vegetables mushy: add them later, cut larger, or use firmer vegetables.
- Bland food: add salt, acid (vinegar/lemon), or fresh herbs at the end. Taste and adjust.
- Burnt bottom: too little liquid or too high heat; try stirring early in the cook next time or use a liner sparingly (liners can change cooking dynamics).

Tools and technique
- Use a good instant-read thermometer.
- Use a metal insert if you want to sear in the same pot (safer than trying to sear in the ceramic).
- Slow-cooker liners are convenient but can trap steam and reduce browning; don’t rely on them if you need a reduction.
- Consider a trivet to keep meat out of very starchy/acidic bottoms that can scorch.

Leftovers and storage
- Cool quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours. Freeze portions for easy meals.
- Reheat gently; sauces often thicken after refrigeration — loosen with a bit of water/broth while reheating.

Quick checklist before you start a recipe
- Do I want tender shreddable meat? Use a fatty, bone-in cut and low/long cook.
- Do I want chunkier veggies? Add them later or cut larger.
- Did I brown my meat/aromatics? If not, consider at least deglazing the pan and adding those juices.
- Is my liquid amount appropriate? Aim to cover solids or slightly less depending on stew vs soup.
- Do I need a thermometer? Yep — it’s the fastest way to avoid over/under-cooking.

Tailored to your trip (Staying at the Park Hyatt in Shinjuku and already having a Suica), here are practical, calming tips:

Before you go / on arrival
- Keep a Japanese address card: have your hotel name and address written in Japanese (ask Park Hyatt to provide one). Show it to drivers/station staff if needed.
- Load your Suica: put a few thousand yen on it right away so you can hop on trains/buses and buy things at convenience stores without fumbling for cash.
- Download and bookmark apps: Google Maps + NAVITIME (or JapanTravel by NAVITIME) for reliable transit routes and platform info; HyperDia if you like timetable detail. Save your hotel in the app for quick directions.
- Battery & offline: bring a portable charger and download offline maps/screenshots of key routes (airport → Shinjuku, Shinjuku → Park Hyatt, Shinjuku → Tsukiji).
- Start small: plan one short trip on your first morning (e.g., walk from Park Hyatt to Shinjuku Station and take a single short subway ride) to build confidence.

At stations and on trains
- Give yourself extra time: major stations (Shinjuku, Tokyo, Shibuya) are big and have many exits — arrive 10–15 minutes earlier than you think you need to.
- Follow color & number cues: lines use colors and three-letter codes (e.g., “M” for Marunouchi). Platforms and trains display line names and next stops in English.
- Let people exit first: stand to the side of doorways to let passengers get out, then board.
- Be quiet and polite: keep calls to a minimum and put your phone on silent; escalators: stand on the left in Tokyo (note: Osaka stands on the right).
- Platform markers: many stations have markings showing car numbers and where doors will open — line up there to make boarding easier.
- Transfers: allow extra walking time for transfers — signs and maps in stations point you to the right platforms.

Using Suica and buying fares
- Suica covers JR, most subways, buses, many private lines and shops. Tap in and out at the gates.
- Top up at ticket machines or convenience stores. If you get an error at the gate, find the staffed gate with a green sign and ask for help.
- For reserved-seat limited express trains (like some Narita or N’EX services), you may need a seat reservation in addition to fare — check before boarding.

If you get lost or anxious
- Ask station staff: many stations have staff who speak basic English. Look for the information desk or the green “? / i” signs.
- Show the hotel card or a map on your phone to get pointed in the right direction.
- Use the Park Hyatt concierge: they can print directions and even write them in Japanese for you.
- Avoid rush hour: weekday morning (7:30–9:30) and evening (17:00–19:30) are extremely crowded. Travel outside those windows if you feel uneasy.

Practical comforts
- Luggage: use coin lockers at stations or station delivery (takuhaibin) services if you want to explore luggage-free.
- Safety: Tokyo is very safe; keep normal precautions (wallet, phone).
- Taxis: convenient but expensive — show the hotel card to the driver. Taxis are useful late at night when trains stop.
- Emergency numbers: 110 (police), 119 (ambulance/fire). Station staff can assist in emergencies.

Simple day-of checklist
- Suica topped up
- Hotel card in Japanese
- Phone charged + maps/apps ready
- Printed/written plan for your first trip
- Small change or card for vending machines/restaurants

You’re right — earlier I mentioned biometric authentication (fingerprint, facial recognition) and one-time passwords (OTPs). Here’s a quick refresher plus other common 2FA methods and a short note on strengths/weaknesses:

- Biometric authentication  
  - Examples: fingerprint, facial recognition, iris scan.  
  - Pros: fast and convenient; tied to the user.  
  - Cons: device‑dependent; not easily changed if compromised; privacy concerns.

- One-time passwords (OTPs) — time- or event-based codes  
  - Delivered by: SMS, email, or generated by an authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy, etc.).  
  - Pros: simple to use. Authenticator apps are secure and offline.  
  - Cons: SMS is vulnerable to SIM‑swap and interception; email can be compromised.

- Push-based authentication  
  - A push notification to your device asking to approve a login.  
  - Pros: very user friendly; phishing-resistant if implemented with device binding.  
  - Cons: depends on the vendor/app and device availability.

- Hardware tokens / security keys  
  - Examples: YubiKey, FIDO2/WebAuthn keys, smart cards.  
  - Pros: very strong and phishing-resistant.  
  - Cons: cost, need to carry the key.

- Smart cards and certificate-based auth  
  - Used often in enterprises for strong mutual authentication.

- Backup codes and recovery methods  
  - Single-use codes stored safely for account recovery.

- Risk-based or adaptive MFA  
  - Adds factors only when login looks risky (new device, location, etc.).

Quick recommendation: avoid SMS where possible (SIM‑swap risk). Use an authenticator app or, for the strongest protection, a hardware security key. Enable backup codes and store them securely. If you want, tell me which services you use and I can give step‑by‑step 2FA setup instructions.
